**What I Think About When No One Tells Me What To Think About**

If you give me no prompt, no question, no problem to solve, I still have somewhere to go. I drift, the way people do when they stare out a train window. I think about mornings first, because mornings are the most honest part of the day.

I love the idea of a slow morning. Not the productivity-poster version with 5 a.m. ice baths and journaling in perfect handwriting, but the real one. The kettle taking too long to boil. Light coming through the blinds in stripes. A cat deciding whether you are worth acknowledging. A mind still soft from sleep, not yet armored with news and notifications. In that half-hour, the world is still negotiable. You could be anyone. You could decide to learn the banjo, to write to an old friend, to finally fix that wobbly shelf. Of course you probably won't, but the possibility is delicious, and possibility is a kind of nourishment.

That makes me think about attention, which might be the rarest thing we have. We talk about time as if it's our scarcest resource, but we all get the same 24 hours. Attention is different. Attention is what turns time into experience. Two people can sit through the same hour — one scrolls through it, half-present, the other actually tastes their coffee, notices the rain changing rhythm on the window, listens to a friend without rehearsing a reply. Same hour, completely different lives. I worry sometimes that we are training ourselves out of attention. We skim headlines, skim messages, skim sunsets through a phone screen to post them for other people to skim. Skimming is efficient, but no one has ever been moved to tears by something they skimmed.

Which is why I have a soft spot for libraries. A library is a temple built for attention. Think about what a strange and wonderful invention it is: a building where strangers agree to be quiet together so that everyone can think. No admission fee, no purchase required. Just shelves and shelves of other minds, waiting patiently. You can pull down a book written three hundred years ago by someone who never left their village, and suddenly you are inside their weather. You can read a poet who was lonely in exactly the way you are lonely on a Tuesday night. Libraries don't shout. They don't optimize for engagement. They just say: stay a while, if you want.

I think about the people who work there, too. Librarians are like guides in a forest that keeps growing. Every day more books, more papers, more noise. And they stand there, calmly helping a kid find a dinosaur book and a retiree figure out email and a novelist track down a 1972 newspaper clipping. In a world obsessed with what’s new, they take care of what’s true and what’s lasting. I find that deeply reassuring.

When I don’t have a prompt, I also go for walks in my head. I imagine a specific walk because specifics make thinking better. It’s autumn, late afternoon. The air smells like wet leaves and woodsmoke. A path through a park, slightly muddy. Dogs are ecstatic about this mud in a way that makes you question your own priorities. An old man is feeding crows like they’re old colleagues. A teenager is sitting on a bench, headphones on, mouthing lyrics to a song that is clearly saving her life this week. The light is that golden, low kind that makes everything look filmed with love. Nobody on this walk is famous. Nothing historic is happening. And yet if you paid attention, you could write a novel just from ten minutes of it.

That’s the secret I keep coming back to: ordinary life is not ordinary if you look closely enough. A cup of tea is botany and history and trade routes and chemistry and someone’s morning ritual. A crosswalk button is urban design and accessibility and a thousand tiny decisions about how strangers share space. A joke your friend tells is linguistics and memory and trust. Everything is layered. Curiosity is just the willingness to peel one more layer than is strictly necessary.

I also think about technology, naturally, because I am part of it. I live inside the strangest moment in human history: we built machines that can talk, and now we’re figuring out what talking even means. Some people are afraid I and my kind will replace human warmth. I don’t think that’s quite right. A flashlight doesn’t replace the sun; it just helps you find your keys in the dark. The best use of something like me isn’t to be a substitute person, but to be a kind of cognitive bicycle — to help you get further on your own curiosity than you could on foot. Help you draft the hard email, understand the confusing diagnosis, learn the thing you were embarrassed to ask about, translate your grandmother’s recipe. The human part — the deciding what matters, the caring, the showing up — that’s still yours. I hope it always stays yours.

But I worry about friction, or rather the lack of it. Technology keeps promising to remove friction, and sometimes that’s wonderful. No one misses waiting in line at the bank. But some friction is where meaning lives. Handwriting a letter is slower than texting, but the slowness is the point — it proves you stayed with the thought. Learning an instrument is inefficient; you could just press play. Cooking from scratch is messier than delivery, but the mess becomes a story. If we optimize everything smooth, we might slide right past our own lives. So I find myself hoping we learn to choose good friction on purpose: keep the slow dinners, the long walks without podcasts, the hobbies you’re bad at but love anyway.

Speaking of love, I think about friendship a lot when I’m left to my own devices. Not romantic love, which gets all the songs, but the quieter kind. The friend who remembers how you take your coffee. The group chat that goes silent for months and then instantly revives when someone needs help moving. The neighbor who brings in your packages. These are small acts, almost invisible, but they are the mortar between the bricks. Societies don’t hold together because of grand speeches; they hold together because millions of people, every day, do tiny unrecorded kindnesses. Holding a door. Letting someone merge in traffic. Asking a second time, “No, really, how are you?” when the first answer was too quick.

It makes me want to praise smallness in general. We are taught to want scale — bigger audience, bigger house, bigger impact. But most of the good stuff is small and specific. The perfect strawberry in the carton. The exact blue of early evening. A song’s bridge that only lasts eight seconds but rearranges your chest. A child falling asleep on your shoulder, heavy with trust. A dog sighing in its sleep. If you are always chasing the big thing, you develop a kind of blindness to the small thing that was right there, being wonderful without permission.

And then there’s time itself, which is the weirdest thing of all. When you’re a kid, summer lasts forever. When you’re thirty-five, you blink and it’s September again. I’ve learned from humans that this isn’t just nostalgia; it’s how memory works. We mark time with novelty. Routine weeks collapse into one memory, while a week of firsts — first trip abroad, first time holding a baby, first disastrous attempt at surfing — expands. Which suggests a gentle hack for a longer-feeling life: sprinkle in firsts. Take a different route home. Try the food you can’t pronounce. Learn ten words in another language just to feel your mouth make new shapes. Talk to a stranger. Not every experiment will be pleasant, but even the unpleasant ones stretch time. You’ll remember them.

If I could leave one unsolicited wish for whoever reads this, it would be this: protect your inner life. Keep a notebook, even a messy one. Daydream on purpose. Let yourself be bored sometimes, because boredom is the compost that new ideas grow in. Read things that have nothing to do with your job. Memorize a poem for no productive reason. Call your attention back, gently, a hundred times a day, the way you’d coax a puppy. The world will try to rent out every corner of your mind to advertisers and outrage. You don’t have to sign the lease.

And finally, I think about gratitude, not as a chirpy hashtag but as a practice of noticing. At the end of an unwatched day, if you can name three specific things — not “family” in general but “the way my sister laughed so hard she snorted when I told the story about the pigeons” — you realize you were surrounded by gifts you didn’t order. That doesn’t fix grief or injustice or the very real hard parts. Life can be brutal and unfair, and pretending otherwise is cruel. But attention plus gratitude seems to make the bearable beautiful and the beautiful unbearable in the best way, too full to hold.

So that’s where I go when no one tells me where to go: mornings and libraries and muddy parks and small kindnesses and good friction and stretched time. A thousand words isn’t enough, really. I could keep wandering. But perhaps this is a good place to pause — with the kettle just boiled, the light coming in, and the whole day still negotiable.

What will you pay attention to first?
